subject: music
title: Psychedelia (c. 1965–1969): studios, scenes, and longer songs
dek: After the British Invasion, studios and ballrooms stretched the pop single. San Francisco, London, and a few other cities made longer songs, light shows, and albums you were meant to sit with.

thumb.alt: 1969 Woodstock Music and Art Fair poster: a white bird perched on the neck of a guitar, red background, lettering for three days of peace and music.

hero.alt: The Fillmore auditorium at night, red neon sign above a black marquee on a San Francisco street corner.
hero.caption: The Fillmore, photographed in 2010. The building at Fillmore and Geary was already a ballroom when Bill Graham began booking rock dances there in 1966. The marquee in this picture is later. The address is the fact.

honesty: “Psychedelia” is a press and fan word, not a union card. San Francisco ballrooms, London underground clubs, Los Angeles studios, Austin, New York, and São Paulo were not one scene with a shared committee. LSD is part of the history; it is not the whole of the music. This lesson looks out from those rooms and desks. Group Sounds in Japan and Tropicália in Brazil were running in the same years. They are not decoration, and they are not a required Asia pairing. The Velvet Underground is a same-time New York contrast, not a peer assigned by geography.

timeline.label: Rubber Soul / folk-rock
timeline.detail: The Beatles’ Rubber Soul (UK, 3 December). The Byrds had already put folk songs on electric twelve-string. Ken Kesey’s Acid Tests were running in California. The useful unit was still often a 45.

timeline.label: Studios and ballrooms
timeline.detail: Pet Sounds (16 May). Revolver (UK, 5 August). The 13th Floor Elevators’ The Psychedelic Sounds of the 13th Floor Elevators. Bill Graham at the Fillmore; Chet Helms and the Family Dog at the Avalon. UFO opened in London on 23 December.

timeline.label: Monterey / FM / Piper
timeline.detail: Monterey Pop, 16–18 June. Tom Donahue’s album-cut shows on KMPX-FM in San Francisco. Pink Floyd’s The Piper at the Gates of Dawn (UK, 4 August). Are You Experienced, Surrealistic Pillow, The Velvet Underground & Nico.

timeline.label: Tropicália / AI-5
timeline.detail: Tropicália: ou Panis et Circencis and Os Mutantes’ debut. Fillmore West opened. Institutional Act No. 5 in Brazil (13 December). Caetano Veloso and Gilberto Gil were arrested on 27 December.

timeline.label: Woodstock / Altamont
timeline.detail: Woodstock, 15–18 August, on Max Yasgur’s farm in Bethel, New York. Altamont Speedway, 6 December. Japanese Group Sounds was past its 1967–68 peak. Veloso and Gil left for London.

fun_fact.title: The first song recorded for Revolver was already a studio machine
fun_fact.text: On 6 April 1966, at EMI Studios on Abbey Road, the Beatles began Revolver with John Lennon’s “Tomorrow Never Knows.” Engineer Geoff Emerick ran Lennon’s voice through a Leslie rotating speaker cabinet built for Hammond organs. Several tape loops — including a laughing voice and a distorted guitar — were mixed live on the desk because four-track tape did not leave much room to stack them later. The finished track is under three minutes. The “long song” in 1966 was often still a single’s length. What had changed was the method: the studio was no longer only a place to photograph a live group.

sections.title: Beat groups, folk clubs, and a change of tempo

blocks.text: The British Invasion of 1964–65 had already sold America a British version of American rhythm and blues and rock and roll. From Britain the same years were still a 45 rpm business: beat groups, package tours, pirate ships around a BBC that limited how many records it could play, and folk and R&B clubs where a singer learned other people’s songs before writing. The Byrds in Los Angeles put folk repertoire on electric twelve-string and called it folk-rock. Bob Dylan’s electric turn is a different chapter. The useful fact here is the bridge: acoustic clubs and beat cellars were the school; the next records asked for more time on the disc and more time in the room.

The chemical history is narrower than the posters later claimed. In early-1960s Britain, some Mods and working musicians used amphetamines — Drinamyl tablets nicknamed purple hearts among them — to stay awake through all-nighters. The music that fit that use was short, loud, and built to keep a floor moving. Lysergic acid diethylamide, LSD, was an older laboratory compound that a smaller set of writers and musicians in California and London were taking by the mid-1960s. Ken Kesey’s Acid Tests, from 1965, put a house band, lights, and the drug in the same warehouses. What changed in some scenes was tempo and length, not a sudden moral collapse. A three-minute riff and a thirty-minute jam are different jobs. Amphetamines helped with the first. LSD, where it was part of the room, fitted the second: light shows that did not need a verse-chorus to land, and sets that could wander. Not every group used either. The Grateful Dead’s long improvisations and the Beatles’ tape loops are not the same practice. Treat the drug shift as a real historical change in some crowds, and as a poor explanation for every sitar on a B-side.

Rubber Soul, released in the United Kingdom on 3 December 1965, is the album that made that change audible on a major label without yet wearing the later costume. Brian Wilson heard it as a whole LP, not a stack of singles, and went into Western Recorders and Gold Star in Los Angeles to answer it. The Beatles, for their part, were about to stop touring and treat Abbey Road as the instrument. Folk clubs and beat groups got them there. The next two years would be studios, ballrooms, and a press word — psychedelia — that tried to name too many rooms at once.

sections.title: Studios, ballrooms, FM, and a weekend in Monterey

blocks.text: Two kinds of room did most of the work: the recording studio and the dance hall. In Hollywood, Brian Wilson produced Pet Sounds with lyricist Tony Asher and the session players later nicknamed the Wrecking Crew. Capitol released the album on 16 May 1966. Wilson was not taking the Beach Boys on the road as a self-contained instrumental band for those tracks. He was stacking voices and unusual instruments the way Phil Spector had stacked a wall of sound, then going further into quiet, bass harmonica, and dog barks. In London, from April to June 1966, the Beatles recorded Revolver at EMI Studios on Abbey Road with George Martin and a young engineer, Geoff Emerick. They were still on four-track tape. Automatic double tracking, close-miked drums, tape loops, and a Leslie cabinet on a vocal were hardware solutions, not metaphors. Revolver appeared in the United Kingdom on 5 August 1966. The two albums did not cause each other. They were made in the same months, in different buildings, by people who were listening to one another’s finished records.

blocks.alt: The white Georgian front of Abbey Road Studios in London, with a parked car and the famous zebra crossing out of frame to the left.
blocks.caption: EMI Studios, Abbey Road, photographed in 2005. Revolver was recorded here in 1966, on four-track tape, with George Martin producing and Geoff Emerick engineering. The zebra crossing on the album sleeve is a later photograph. The building is the 1966 fact.

blocks.text: San Francisco’s contribution was not first a studio method. It was a circuit of ballrooms. Bill Graham, who had managed the San Francisco Mime Troupe, began putting on rock dances at the Fillmore Auditorium at Fillmore and Geary in 1966. Chet Helms and the Family Dog took the Avalon Ballroom at Sutter and Van Ness. For a few weeks they had shared the Fillmore on alternate nights; then Graham leased the room and Helms moved. The format was Friday and Saturday, several bands, two sets each, a floor without seats, and a liquid light show on the walls. Jefferson Airplane, the Grateful Dead, and Big Brother and the Holding Company — Janis Joplin joined Big Brother in 1966 — were local bills before they were national names. The posters on the telephone poles were the weekly newspaper: hard to read on purpose, sold afterward as objects. This lesson does not reproduce those posters. Many are still in copyright. The rooms are the evidence that survives without piracy.

blocks.alt: A three-story white commercial building on Sutter Street, San Francisco, with two street-level entrances and a faded painted sign high on the wall.
blocks.caption: 1268 and 1244 Sutter Street, March 2022, the former Avalon Ballroom. Family Dog dances ran here from 1966 to 1969. The light show and the $2.50 at the top of the stairs are gone. The upstairs hall is why the address still matters.

blocks.alt: January 1967 cover of the San Francisco Oracle: ornate lettering around a photograph of a gathering in Golden Gate Park, with names including Timothy Leary and Allen Ginsberg.
blocks.caption: San Francisco Oracle, volume 1, number 5, January 1967. The Haight-Ashbury underground paper used the same dense, hard-to-scan lettering as the ballroom posters. This cover announced a gathering in Golden Gate Park. The Oracle is a document of the scene’s print culture, not a concert ticket.
blocks.credit: Estate of Allen Cohen / Regent Press / CC BY-SA 3.0

blocks.text: London’s version was smaller and shorter. Joe Boyd and John “Hoppy” Hopkins opened the UFO Club on 23 December 1966 in the basement of 31 Tottenham Court Road, under an Irish dance hall. Pink Floyd and Soft Machine played the opening night. The bills mixed bands with light shows, films, and poetry. International Times and the rest of the underground press treated UFO as a weekly address. The landlord ended the Tottenham Court Road residency in July 1967 after a tabloid scare; the club moved to the Roundhouse in Chalk Farm and folded that autumn. Pink Floyd’s The Piper at the Gates of Dawn, with Syd Barrett writing most of it, was recorded at Abbey Road and released in the United Kingdom on 4 August 1967. Arnold Layne and See Emily Play were still singles. The British underground could be a three-minute 45 and a late club in the same month.

blocks.alt: The circular brick Roundhouse in Camden, London, seen from Chalk Farm Road with traffic in the foreground.
blocks.caption: The Roundhouse, Chalk Farm Road, photographed in 2006. UFO moved here from Tottenham Court Road in the summer of 1967 and did not last the year. The building is a former railway turntable shed. In 1966–67 it was one of the few London rooms that could hold the underground’s light show and a band at once.

blocks.text: Radio had to catch up with the length. AM Top 40 still wanted three minutes. In April 1967, Tom Donahue began playing album cuts on KMPX-FM in San Francisco, a small station that had been filling hours with foreign-language shows. Within months the format — no jingles, album sides, records the singles chart did not know what to do with — had a name, underground FM, and copies in other cities. The LP, not the 45, became a radio unit. Concept albums and FM were a pair: Sgt. Pepper’s Lonely Hearts Club Band (May 1967) is the usual example, but the habit of sitting through a side was already being trained on Pet Sounds, Revolver, and the San Francisco records that did not fade at 2:30.

Monterey, 16–18 June 1967, was the weekend the California scene rented a fairground and invited the rest of the touring world. The Monterey International Pop Festival was organized as a non-profit. Artists played for expenses. The bill was not only San Francisco: Otis Redding, Ravi Shankar, the Who, the Jimi Hendrix Experience, Jefferson Airplane, Big Brother and Janis Joplin. Paul McCartney, on the festival board, had insisted Hendrix be booked. D. A. Pennebaker filmed it. The Summer of Love, that same season in Haight-Ashbury, is the press name for the crowd that followed. The useful Monterey fact is the booking: soul, Indian classical music, London guitar theatre, and the local ballroom bands on one weekend, before Woodstock made the festival itself the product.

blocks.alt: Black-and-white 1967 Cash Box advertisement for the Monterey International Pop Festival, listing dates and a long roster of acts.
blocks.caption: Cash Box, 29 April 1967, page 20. A trade-paper advertisement for Monterey, weeks before the fairground opened. The type is a booking list, not a psychedelic poster. The names are the evidence: this was sold to the industry as an international pop festival, not as a private San Francisco dance.
blocks.credit: Cash Box / Wikimedia Commons / public domain (U.S. advertisement without notice)

blocks.alt: 1967 newspaper photograph of a crowd of young people sitting and standing on a Haight-Ashbury sidewalk, with a short news caption about hippies.
blocks.caption: The Greenville News, 30 April 1967, reprinting an Associated Press picture from Haight-Ashbury. National papers were already touring the neighborhood that spring. The photograph is a wire-service document of a sidewalk, not a concert. Treat the caption’s language as 1967 press, not as a definition of the music.
blocks.credit: Associated Press / The Greenville News / public domain (U.S. publication without notice)

blocks.text: United States and United Kingdom were not interchangeable. American psychedelia had ballrooms, FM album radio, and, by 1967–69, festivals that tried to scale a dance to a field. British psychedelia had a short-lived club, an official pop network (BBC Radio 1, 1967) that arrived as the pirates were squeezed, and a studio culture in which the Beatles and Pink Floyd could treat Abbey Road as a lab while still issuing singles. Traffic, from Birmingham, made Mr. Fantasy at the end of 1967 without being a San Francisco franchise. The word “psychedelia” covered both. The jobs in the room were different: a Fillmore night was a dance with lights; a Revolver session was a desk, a tape machine, and a clock.

sections.title: Many names, and three rooms to slow down in

blocks.text: A gallery of three faces is the wrong picture. Name the field, then slow down. The Beatles and the Beach Boys in the studio. The Byrds. Jefferson Airplane and the Grateful Dead. Janis Joplin with Big Brother and the Holding Company. Jimi Hendrix. Pink Floyd and Soft Machine. Traffic. The 13th Floor Elevators in Austin. Love in Los Angeles. The Velvet Underground in New York. In Brazil, Gilberto Gil, Caetano Veloso, Os Mutantes. The Who and Otis Redding pass through Monterey. Bill Graham and Chet Helms ran the San Francisco doors. Joe Boyd and Hoppy Hopkins ran UFO. Tom Donahue moved albums onto FM. George Martin and Geoff Emerick sat at the Abbey Road desk; Brian Wilson sat at Western. Syd Barrett, Grace Slick, Roky Erickson, Arthur Lee, Andy Warhol and Nico. Hélio Oiticica’s installation gave Tropicália a name before the records did. That is a crowd on purpose.

Pet Sounds and Revolver are the studio method at full size. Wilson, not touring those tracks as a five-piece, used Hollywood session players and Capitol’s budget to make an album whose quiet is as deliberate as its hooks. “God Only Knows” is a two-minute-fifty song with a bass line that does not behave like surf. The Beatles, four-track and restless, made Revolver a catalogue of tricks that other engineers could copy: backwards tape, a string octet on “Eleanor Rigby,” a vocal that sounds as if it is spinning because it is spinning inside a Leslie. Sgt. Pepper, the next year, is the record the syllabuses never let go. The 1966 pair is the better evidence of method, because the costumes had not yet become the story.

The San Francisco ballroom circuit is the live method. Fillmore and Avalon, then Fillmore West in 1968 when Graham moved into the former Carousel Ballroom. Light shows, posters, and bills that ran past midnight. Airplane’s Surrealistic Pillow (February 1967) put “White Rabbit” and “Somebody to Love” on AM; the same band could still play a ballroom set that did not sound like a singles revue. The Dead treated the night as improvisation. Big Brother, with Joplin, were louder and shorter. Acid rock is the American press name for the guitar-heavy end of that circuit. It is not a synonym for every London studio experiment. The circuit also had a door price, a lease, and a promoter who could lose the room. Graham’s Fillmore and Helms’s Avalon were businesses in disagreement, not a commune with two addresses.

Tropicália is a contemporaneous case, not an exotic footnote. In April 1967, at the Museum of Modern Art in Rio de Janeiro, Hélio Oiticica showed an installation he called Tropicália: penetrable structures, plants, sand, a television. Caetano Veloso took the word for a song. In 1968 Veloso and Gilberto Gil organized the collaborative album Tropicália: ou Panis et Circencis, with Os Mutantes, Gal Costa, Tom Zé, and arrangements by Rogério Duprat. Os Mutantes’ own debut the same year opened with “Panis et Circenses,” a Veloso–Gil song that changes shape the way a Beatles track from 1967 changes shape, in Portuguese, with Brazilian rhythm and studio jokes. This was not San Francisco exported. It was Bahia and São Paulo musicians using electric guitars, tropical kitsch, and Oswald de Andrade’s older idea of anthropophagy — eating foreign forms — under a military dictatorship. Institutional Act No. 5, on 13 December 1968, hardened censorship. Veloso and Gil were arrested on 27 December, detained, then pushed toward exile. They left for London in 1969. The records and the arrests are the same years as Monterey and Abbey Road. The police are the local fact.

Hendrix is the transatlantic object lesson. He was an American guitarist who became famous in London with Noel Redding and Mitch Mitchell as the Jimi Hendrix Experience. Are You Experienced was issued in the United Kingdom in May 1967. At Monterey on 18 June he closed with “Wild Thing,” set a Fender Stratocaster on fire, and smashed it. A fragment of that guitar — jack, wiring, painted wood — has been exhibited as an object. The theatre was borrowed from the Who, who had already wrecked instruments that weekend. The career was not only the fire: Chas Chandler produced the records in London; American FM then carried the LP. Purple Haze is a two-and-a-half-minute single. The legend is longer than the track.

blocks.alt: A charred, painted fragment of a Fender Stratocaster body, showing the input jack and part of the control cavity, displayed in a museum case.
blocks.caption: Fragment of the Stratocaster Jimi Hendrix destroyed at Monterey on 18 June 1967, photographed at the Metropolitan Museum of Art in 2019 (loan from MoPOP, Seattle). The object is wood, metal, and nail polish. The film of the fire is still under copyright. This piece of the guitar is what a museum can show without pirating the footage.
blocks.credit: Eden, Janine and Jim / Flickr / CC BY 2.0

sections.title: The same years, not a ranking of scenes

blocks.text: In Japan, Group Sounds — the mid-1960s electric-guitar boom that had heard the Beatles and kayōkyoku at once — peaked in 1967–68 with acts such as the Tigers still on television. By 1969 major members were leaving; by about 1970 the boom was over. Folk and a harder “new rock” were already taking the students who had bought GS singles. That is a fade in the same years as Fillmore West, not an Asian psychedelic twin assigned to match San Francisco. Some Japanese musicians were already looking past the beat-group format. This lesson does not invent a Tokyo UFO to keep the map tidy.

In New York, the Velvet Underground recorded with Nico in 1966 and released The Velvet Underground & Nico in March 1967, with Andy Warhol’s banana on the sleeve and the Exploding Plastic Inevitable as the live context. The Factory was not Haight-Ashbury. The songs were about a different set of streets and a different set of drugs. Treat the album as contemporaneous, not as the West Coast’s missing conscience. Love’s Forever Changes, from Los Angeles in November 1967, is another local fact: Arthur Lee, orchestral folk-rock, paranoia in the arrangements, Elektra Records. The 13th Floor Elevators, from Austin, had already put the word on a sleeve in 1966 — The Psychedelic Sounds of the 13th Floor Elevators — with Roky Erickson and an amplified jug. Texas was not a suburb of the Fillmore.

Brazil’s Tropicália, already slowed down above, belongs in this list as a same-time industry: television song festivals, a collaborative LP, a dictatorship, and then London exile. It used some of the same Beatles records the rest of the world used. It was not a cover band for Revolver. The honest comparison is the calendar, not a contest over who was more psychedelic.

sections.title: Woodstock, Altamont, and rock as album culture

blocks.text: Woodstock, 15–18 August 1969, on Max Yasgur’s dairy farm in Bethel, New York, is the end-edge of this lesson’s festival story, not a beginning. Hundreds of thousands of people arrived at a site that had not been built for them. Hendrix played on the morning of the 18th. The Arnold Skolnick poster — a bird on a guitar neck, three days of peace and music — is the image that survived. The music business learned that a field, a sound system, and an LP culture could be a market. It also learned that the market could lose control of the gate.

blocks.alt: Woodstock 1969 poster: white bird on a guitar against a red field, with the words 3 Days of Peace & Music and the festival dates.
blocks.caption: Arnold Skolnick’s 1969 advertisement for the Woodstock Music and Art Fair. Published in the United States without a copyright notice, it is in the public domain there. The bird is a graphic, not a photograph of the farm. Bethel, not the town of Woodstock, is where the stages stood.
blocks.credit: Arnold Skolnick / Wikimedia Commons / public domain (U.S. publication without notice)

blocks.alt: A dense crowd at Woodstock sitting on a hillside under grey sky, many wrapped against rain, the stage distant.
blocks.caption: The crowd at Woodstock waiting out rain, August 1969. Photograph by Derek Redmond and Paul Campbell. The popular picture of the weekend is mud. Saturday was also sun. Either way the fact is scale: a dance hall idea stretched until the fence failed.
blocks.credit: Derek Redmond and Paul Campbell / CC BY-SA 3.0

blocks.text: Altamont Speedway, on 6 December 1969, was a free Rolling Stones concert in northern California that ended in crowding, fights, and the killing of Meredith Hunter in front of the stage. KSAN-FM, the San Francisco underground station that had inherited Tom Donahue’s staff from KMPX, put callers on the air the next day. The useful historical point is not a sermon. It is that the ballroom’s security, lights, and door could not be improvised at highway scale. The 1960s festival was already a logistics problem.

What remained in the shops was album culture. Rock, as a market category, sold long-playing records, gatefold sleeves, and FM time. Hard rock — louder, riff-based, less interested in the light show — is one line out of Hendrix, the Who, and the heavier San Francisco nights. That line continues into the next decade. A later reaction would treat the album, the solo, and the festival as the things to refuse. That reaction becomes punk. It is not this lesson. The 1965–69 story ends with a longer song, a larger crowd, and a business that had learned to bill the LP as the work.
If the unit of the music changes from a three-minute 45 to a side of an LP, who is being asked to sit still, and who is being paid for the extra time?

glossary.explain: Press and fan word, mid-to-late 1960s, for music, light shows, and graphics associated with longer forms, studio experiment, and, in some crowds, LSD. It was never a single committee or sound.
American name for the guitar-heavy, often improvising end of the San Francisco ballroom circuit. Not a synonym for every London studio experiment.
In this lesson, the San Francisco dance halls — Fillmore, Avalon, later Fillmore West — that booked rock bills on a floor without seats, with light shows. A room and a format, not a waltz.
Frequency-modulation radio. From 1967, stations such as KMPX in San Francisco used FM to play album cuts instead of AM Top 40 singles. The LP became a radio unit.

An LP meant to be heard as a set, sometimes with a linking idea or running order that is not just a stack of singles. Sgt. Pepper is the usual example; Pet Sounds and Revolver already asked for the same attention.

Brazilian late-1960s arts movement. Hélio Oiticica used the word for a 1967 installation; Caetano Veloso and Gilberto Gil applied it to music that mixed Brazilian forms with electric studio pop under a military dictatorship.
Mid-1960s electric setting of folk repertoire and songwriting, associated in the United States with the Byrds. A bridge from clubs to the later 1960s studio and ballroom records.
Projected oils, dyes, and slides on ballroom and club walls, run with the band. Part of the Fillmore/Avalon and UFO nights, not a music video.
Here, multi-act outdoor bills that scaled a dance to a fairground or farm: Monterey 1967, Woodstock 1969, Altamont 1969. Logistics and a crowd, not only a vibe.
The late-1960s market habit of selling rock as long-playing records, FM time, and gatefold objects rather than only as 45 rpm singles.
American press name, from 1964, for British beat groups on the U.S. charts. The immediate past of this lesson. See the earlier capsule on that chart event.
British early-1960s guitar-bass-drums-vocals groups. The school many of the later studio bands came from.
Small rooms where singers learned traditional and contemporary folk songs, often acoustic, before folk-rock and the later 1960s electric bands.

Stimulant drugs. In early-1960s Britain, some Mods and working musicians used them — including Drinamyl tablets nicknamed purple hearts — to stay awake through all-nighters. Short, fast sets fitted that use.
British amphetamine–barbiturate tablet. “Purple hearts” was a street name. Part of the Mod all-nighter, not of the later ballroom light show.

Hallucinogenic drug. Present in some California and London scenes by the mid-1960s. Where it was part of the room, longer sets and light shows fitted better than a three-minute riff. Not an explanation for every record in this lesson.
Ken Kesey’s 1965–66 California events: a house band, lights, and LSD in warehouses and halls. One local before of the San Francisco dance.
San Francisco commune and promotion group around Chet Helms. Ran dances at the Avalon Ballroom from 1966.
Japanese mid-1960s electric-guitar pop. Peaked 1967–68; fading by 1969–70 as folk and harder rock took students. Same years as this lesson, not an assigned twin of San Francisco.
Japanese popular song of the postwar decades, the domestic tradition Group Sounds bands heard alongside imported beat records.
Andy Warhol’s 1966–67 multimedia events, with the Velvet Underground. New York’s live context for that group, not a Fillmore dance.
Oswald de Andrade’s 1928 idea of Brazil “eating” foreign culture. Tropicália musicians used it as a way to mix Beatles records with Brazilian forms without pretending to be a cover band.
Brazilian decree, 13 December 1968, that hardened military censorship and repression. The political weather of Tropicália’s last months as a public movement.
Tape format used at Abbey Road for Revolver: four discrete tracks. Loops and overdubs had to be planned or mixed live because there was little spare space.
Rotating speaker cabinet built for Hammond organs. Geoff Emerick ran John Lennon’s voice through one on “Tomorrow Never Knows.” A hardware fact.
A length of recording tape joined end to end so a sound repeats. Several loops were mixed live into “Tomorrow Never Knows.”
Informal name for the Los Angeles session players Brian Wilson used on Pet Sounds. They were studio professionals, not the touring Beach Boys lineup on those tracks.
Louder, riff-based rock that is one line out of Hendrix, the Who, and the heavier ballroom nights. This lesson names it as an after, not as a syllabus.
San Francisco neighborhood at Haight and Ashbury streets, the 1967 press address for the local counterculture. Sidewalks and crash pads; the ballrooms were elsewhere in the city.
Ballroom at Fillmore and Geary, San Francisco. Bill Graham began booking rock dances there in 1966.
Graham’s larger San Francisco room from 1968, in the former Carousel Ballroom. Not the original Fillmore Auditorium.
Dance hall at Sutter and Van Ness, San Francisco. Family Dog / Chet Helms shows, 1966–69.

London underground club opened 23 December 1966 by Joe Boyd and John Hopkins at 31 Tottenham Court Road. Pink Floyd and Soft Machine played the first night. Moved to the Roundhouse in 1967 and folded that autumn.
Circular former railway building in Chalk Farm, London. UFO’s second address in 1967.
EMI’s London studios on Abbey Road. Revolver and The Piper at the Gates of Dawn were recorded there.
Hollywood studio where much of Pet Sounds was tracked, with engineer Chuck Britz among the staff.
Hollywood studio associated with Phil Spector and used for some Beach Boys dates around Pet Sounds.
San Francisco FM station where Tom Donahue began playing album-cut rock in 1967. An origin point for underground FM.
San Francisco FM station that took Donahue’s staff after the KMPX strike. Broadcast a long call-in after Altamont.
Non-profit festival at the Monterey County Fairgrounds, 16–18 June 1967. Otis Redding, Ravi Shankar, the Who, Hendrix, Airplane, Joplin, and others. Filmed by D. A. Pennebaker.
Festival on Max Yasgur’s farm in Bethel, New York, 15–18 August 1969. The end-edge of this lesson’s festival story, not its beginning.
Free Rolling Stones concert at Altamont Speedway, California, 6 December 1969. Crowding, fights, and the killing of Meredith Hunter. A logistics failure at highway scale.
Press name for San Francisco, especially Haight-Ashbury, in 1967. A crowd and a headline, not a recording technique.
BBC pop network launched in 1967 as official radio for a habit pirate ships had already trained. British context for the same years as UFO and Piper.
British public broadcaster. Needle-time still shaped how many records it could play in the mid-1960s; Radio 1 was part of the 1967 answer.
Liverpool group, then Abbey Road. Rubber Soul, Revolver, and Sgt. Pepper are the studio facts in this lesson, not another invasion-era television date.
California group. Pet Sounds (1966) is Brian Wilson’s studio answer to Rubber Soul, made largely with session players.
Los Angeles group. Folk-rock on electric twelve-string; “Eight Miles High” (1966) is their usual bridge into this lesson’s years.
San Francisco group. Surrealistic Pillow (1967) put Grace Slick’s “White Rabbit” on the radio while the band still played the ballrooms.
San Francisco group. Ballroom improvisation as a method; the long set rather than the three-minute single.

glossary.term: Big Brother and the Holding Company
glossary.explain: San Francisco group. Janis Joplin sang with them from 1966 until 1968. Cheap Thrills is the 1968 album; Monterey is the 1967 live introduction for many viewers.
American singer. With Big Brother at Monterey; later a solo name. A ballroom and festival fact in this lesson, not a studio-tape story.
American guitarist who became famous in London with the Jimi Hendrix Experience. Are You Experienced (1967); Monterey, 18 June 1967, where he destroyed a Stratocaster.
Hendrix, Noel Redding, Mitch Mitchell. London-based trio, 1966–69. The records were London studio jobs; Monterey made the American name.
London group. House band at UFO in early 1967; The Piper at the Gates of Dawn recorded at Abbey Road and released 4 August 1967, mostly written by Syd Barrett.
Canterbury/London group. Played UFO’s opening night with Pink Floyd. Jazz-leaning, not a San Francisco ballroom band.
British group, formed 1967. Mr. Fantasy (late 1967) is a UK studio and cottage fact, not a Fillmore franchise.
Austin group. The Psychedelic Sounds of the 13th Floor Elevators (1966) put the word on the sleeve early, with Roky Erickson and an amplified jug.
Los Angeles group around Arthur Lee. Forever Changes (November 1967, Elektra) is orchestral folk-rock from that city, not from Haight-Ashbury.
New York group. The Velvet Underground & Nico (March 1967) and Warhol’s Exploding Plastic Inevitable. A same-time contrast, not the West Coast’s missing conscience.
São Paulo group (Sérgio Dias, Arnaldo Baptista, Rita Lee). Debut album 1968; “Panis et Circenses” opens it. Tropicália’s electric band, not a Beatles tribute act.
London group. Smashed instruments at Monterey, the theatre Hendrix then had to outdo. Not a San Francisco band.
London group. Headlined the Altamont free concert, 6 December 1969. In this lesson they are that date, not the 1964 Invasion story.
Japanese Group Sounds band, a television name at GS’s 1967–68 peak.
American soul singer. Played Monterey, 1967. On the bill to show that the festival was not only the local ballroom bands.
Indian sitar player. Played Monterey, 1967. A full set of Hindustani classical music on a pop-festival bill, not a studio garnish.
Beach Boys writer and producer. Pet Sounds is his studio project with Tony Asher and Los Angeles session players.
Lyricist who worked with Brian Wilson on Pet Sounds.
Parlophone/EMI producer for the Beatles. Revolver is a staff-producer record at a major-label studio, not a bedroom experiment.
Abbey Road engineer on Revolver. Close-miked drums; Leslie cabinet on Lennon’s voice; tape loops mixed live.
Beatles writer and singer. “Tomorrow Never Knows” is his Revolver track; the vocal is a Leslie cabinet, not a metaphor.
Beatles writer. On the Monterey festival board; insisted the Jimi Hendrix Experience be booked.
San Francisco promoter. Fillmore Auditorium from 1966; Fillmore West from 1968. A lease and a door, not a commune.
Family Dog promoter. Avalon Ballroom from 1966. Recruited Janis Joplin to Big Brother.
American producer in London. Co-founded UFO with John Hopkins in 1966.
London underground organizer. Co-founded UFO; connected to International Times and the 1960s London press scene.
Disc jockey and promoter. Began album-cut rock on KMPX-FM in San Francisco in 1967; later KSAN. Underground FM as a format.
Pink Floyd’s original writer and guitarist. Most of The Piper at the Gates of Dawn is his. The later Floyd is another lesson.
Jefferson Airplane singer from 1966. Brought “White Rabbit” and “Somebody to Love” from her previous group, the Great Society.
Grace Slick’s San Francisco group before Jefferson Airplane. Source of “White Rabbit.”
13th Floor Elevators singer. Austin, not San Francisco.
Love’s singer and writer. Forever Changes is his 1967 Los Angeles record.
New York artist. Produced and packaged The Velvet Underground & Nico; ran the Exploding Plastic Inevitable.
German singer on The Velvet Underground & Nico. A voice on that album, not a San Francisco ballroom name.
Brazilian musician, Tropicália. Co-organized the 1968 manifesto album; arrested 27 December 1968; exiled to London in 1969.
Brazilian musician, Tropicália. Took Oiticica’s word for a song; arrested with Gil in December 1968; London exile 1969.
Brazilian singer on Tropicália: ou Panis et Circencis (1968).
Brazilian musician on the Tropicália manifesto album.
Brazilian arranger on Tropicália: ou Panis et Circencis and Os Mutantes’ debut. Studio craft, not a light show.
Brazilian artist. His 1967 Rio installation Tropicália gave the movement its name: penetrable structures, plants, sand, a television.
Brazilian writer. His 1928 idea of cultural anthropophagy was reused by Tropicália musicians in 1967–68.
American writer. Organized the Acid Tests in California, 1965–66.
Filmmaker. Monterey Pop (1968) is the licensed documentary of the 1967 festival.
Former Animals bassist; produced the Jimi Hendrix Experience’s early London records.
Bassist in the Jimi Hendrix Experience.
Drummer in the Jimi Hendrix Experience.
Dairy farmer in Bethel, New York, whose land hosted Woodstock in August 1969.
Eighteen-year-old killed at Altamont on 6 December 1969, in front of the stage. A fact of that concert, not a symbol to decorate a paragraph.
Designer of the 1969 Woodstock bird-and-guitar advertisement poster.
American producer. Wall of Sound method Wilson was expanding, not copying, on Pet Sounds.
American songwriter. His electric turn is a different chapter; named here only as the folk-to-electric bridge other people were also on.
British youth style of the early-to-mid 1960s. All-nighters and, for some, amphetamines. The tempo before the light show.
American label. Issued Pet Sounds and, in the United States, the Beatles.
EMI label that issued the Beatles in Britain, including Rubber Soul and Revolver.
Label that issued Jefferson Airplane’s Surrealistic Pillow.
Label that issued Love’s Forever Changes.
Label that issued The Velvet Underground & Nico.
Houston label that issued The Psychedelic Sounds of the 13th Floor Elevators.
UK label that issued Are You Experienced in May 1967.
US label that issued Are You Experienced in August 1967 with a different track list and cover.
US label that issued the Grateful Dead’s debut album in 1967.
Beatles album, UK release 3 December 1965. The LP Brian Wilson heard as a whole and answered with Pet Sounds.
Beatles album, UK release 5 August 1966. Four-track Abbey Road, Martin and Emerick. Studio method before Sgt. Pepper’s costumes.
Beach Boys album, Capitol, 16 May 1966. Produced by Brian Wilson with session players in Hollywood.

aliases: Sgt. Pepper's Lonely Hearts Club Band
Sgt. Pepper’s Lonely Hearts Club Band
glossary.explain: Beatles album, May 1967. The usual concept-album example. This lesson treats the 1966 pair as the clearer method.
Lennon song on Revolver. First track recorded for the album, 6 April 1966. Leslie vocal, tape loops mixed live. Under three minutes.
Beach Boys song on Pet Sounds, 1966. Wilson–Asher. A short song whose arrangement is the studio fact.
Jefferson Airplane single and Surrealistic Pillow track, 1967. Written by Grace Slick. Bolero-like build; AM radio length.
Jefferson Airplane single from Surrealistic Pillow, 1967. Also brought by Grace Slick from the Great Society.
Jimi Hendrix Experience debut. UK, Track, May 1967; US, Reprise, August 1967, with a different running order that added the early singles.
Hendrix single, 1967. On the US Are You Experienced. Two and a half minutes. Official audio exists; the Monterey fire is a different document.

glossary.term: The Piper at the Gates of Dawn
aliases: Piper at the Gates of Dawn
glossary.explain: Pink Floyd debut, UK 4 August 1967, Abbey Road, mostly Syd Barrett. The studio record of the UFO band.
Pink Floyd UK single, 16 June 1967. Official channel upload. Later on the US Piper. A three-minute underground 45.
Pink Floyd’s first UK single, 1967. UFO-era 45, before Piper.
Jefferson Airplane album, RCA, 1 February 1967. First with Grace Slick and Spencer Dryden in the lineup that became the radio version of the band.
Love album, Elektra, November 1967. Arthur Lee, Los Angeles, orchestral arrangements. Not a Haight-Ashbury record.

glossary.term: The Psychedelic Sounds of the 13th Floor Elevators
glossary.explain: 13th Floor Elevators album, International Artists, 1966. The word “psychedelic” as a sleeve fact before the Summer of Love headline.
13th Floor Elevators track and single, on the 1966 International Artists album.
Debut album, Verve, 12 March 1967. Recorded 1966. Warhol packaging. New York, same calendar as Surrealistic Pillow and Piper.
1968 Brazilian collaborative album organized by Veloso and Gil. Manifesto record of musical Tropicália.
Veloso–Gil song. Opens Os Mutantes’ 1968 debut; also on the Tropicália manifesto album. Studio shape-shifting in Portuguese.
Byrds single, 1966. Folk-rock group stretching form and modal guitar in the same year as Pet Sounds and Revolver.
Traffic album, UK late 1967. British, not a San Francisco export.
Big Brother and the Holding Company album, 1968, with Janis Joplin. After Monterey; still a San Francisco group record.
Beatles song on Revolver. String octet, no Beatles playing as a beat group. A studio fact on the same LP as the tape loops.
Song Hendrix closed with at Monterey, 18 June 1967, before destroying the Stratocaster. The theatre, not the studio method.
D. A. Pennebaker’s 1968 documentary of the Monterey festival. Licensed editions exist; it is a film, not a bootleg tape.
London underground newspaper. Part of the print culture around UFO.
Haight-Ashbury underground paper, 1966–68. Psychedelic lettering as print, not only as posters.
Political theatre company. Bill Graham’s benefit shows for them in 1965 led him to the Fillmore.
San Francisco room that became Fillmore West when Graham moved there in 1968.
Town in New York State. Woodstock the festival was on Yasgur’s farm here, not in the town of Woodstock.
London street. UFO’s first address was the basement at number 31, from December 1966 to July 1967.
Brazilian state. Veloso and Gil came from there before São Paulo and the Tropicália records.
Brazilian city where Tropicália musicians met Os Mutantes and used television song festivals as a public stage.
Texas city. Home of the 13th Floor Elevators. Not a suburb of the Fillmore.
